newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil shrs post biggest one-day drop since Jan 95.
newsitem.headline: Brazil shrs post biggest one-day drop since Jan 95.

text.p: Brazil shares closed sharply lower on Tuesday, with the Bovespa index posting its largest single-day drop in terms of percentage since January 1995, when stocks tumbled after the Mexican peso devaluation.
Sao Paulo's Bovespa index ended 8.51 percent lower at 11,617 points. Turnover was 1.41 billion reais ($1.30 billion).

Brokers said a combination of factors, including local wire reports on comments by a key government minister criticizing a senior central bank official, led to the bolsa closing near its lowest point of the day.

The market's retreat was led by individual investors in domestic equity funds, particularly those who joined the funds in May and June to take advantage of the bolsa's powerful advance since the beginning of 1997, analysts said.

Those investors, who had moved from fixed-income investments to stock funds seeking higher returns, booked profits on Tuesday, rattled by newspaper headlines on the bolsa's sharp decline in the previous two days, analysts said.
"Basically investors originally from fixed-income funds that are withdrawing their money from the bolsa," said Angelo Romano, capital markets director at Rio de Janeiro-based Banco Boavista.

The selling spree, in which the bourse lost 14.6 percent over three sessions, was triggered by fears that speculative attacks that forced some Asian countries to devalue their currencies in recent weeks could also spread to Brazil.
But analysts said there were no economic fundamentals to support the market's nosedive.
"Nothing justifies a drop of these proportions. The market has overreacted," said Deiwes Rubira de Assis, vice-president at ING Barings, Brazil.

Observers say that Brazil suffers from some of the same economic ills -- a widening current account gap and overvalued currency -- that made some Asian nations vulnerable to currency speculators. Thailand and the Philippines have been forced into de facto devaluations.
But Brazil has $59 billion in foreign reserves to ward off any speculative attack on its currency, the real.

Local wire reports on comments by Communications Minister Sergio Motta criticizing Gustavo Franco, who is in charge of Brazil's foreign exchange policy, also prompted unease, particularly late in the session.
Bellwether Telebras plummeted 8.23 percent to close at 145 reais, and state oil company Petrobras closed off 8.17 percent at 281 reais. The mining concern CVRD plunged 7.75 percent to 25 reais.
Traders said the market should continue to be unsettled over the next two or three sessions but was likely to begin recovering by the end of the week.
